questions.question: Which feature of xylem vessels makes them suitable for transporting water from the roots to the leaves? A cross walls with pores (sieve plates) between adjacent cells, B living cytoplasm with many mitochondria, C walls strengthened with lignin and no end walls between adjacent cells, D thin walls made only of cellulose.
questions.answer: C: walls strengthened with lignin and no end walls between adjacent cells
steps: Lignin makes the walls strong and waterproof, so the vessels do not collapse and water does not leak out.
Xylem vessels are dead and have no end walls, so they form a continuous hollow tube with little resistance to the flow of water.
A describes phloem sieve tubes, B describes companion cells, and D is wrong because xylem walls are thickened with lignin.

questions.question: Which statement about phloem tissue is correct? A Sieve tube elements contain many mitochondria and a large nucleus, B Companion cells have many mitochondria to provide ATP for loading sucrose into the sieve tube elements, C Sieve plates are made of lignin and allow the transport of water, D Phloem transports water and mineral ions from the roots to the leaves.
questions.answer: B: companion cells have many mitochondria to provide ATP for loading sucrose into the sieve tube elements
steps: Companion cells are metabolically active and have many mitochondria, which provide ATP for the active loading of sucrose into the sieve tube elements.
A is wrong because sieve tube elements have very little cytoplasm and no nucleus.
C is wrong because sieve plates are perforated cross walls (not lignified) that allow the sucrose solution to pass.
D describes xylem; phloem transports organic solutes such as sucrose.

questions.question: Explain how a lack of nitrate ions in the soil would reduce the growth of a plant.
questions.answer: Nitrate provides the nitrogen for amino acids and nucleotides, so fewer proteins and nucleic acids can be made for new cells and growth is stunted.
steps: Nitrate provides the nitrogen for amino acids, which are joined to make proteins (including enzymes)
Nitrogen is needed for nucleotides (DNA, RNA), so cell division is limited
Fewer new cells / less protein synthesis, so growth is stunted
accept: Nitrogen is a component of chlorophyll, so photosynthesis is reduced
Older leaves turn yellow as nitrogen is moved to the growing regions
Nitrogen is also needed for ATP and NADP

questions.question: In an investigation of the tensile strength of plant fibres, masses were added to each fibre until it broke. Fibre A, of diameter 0.25 mm, broke when the mass supported was 1.8 kg. Fibre B, of diameter 0.40 mm, broke when the mass supported was 4.2 kg. Calculate the breaking mass per mm2 of cross-sectional area for each fibre, to 2 significant figures, and state which fibre has the greater tensile strength.
questions.answer: Fibre A: 37 kg mm^-2; fibre B: 33 kg mm^-2; fibre A has the greater tensile strength
steps: Cross-sectional area of A = pi x 0.125^2 = 0.0491 mm2; breaking mass per mm2 = 1.8 / 0.0491 = 37 kg mm^-2.
Cross-sectional area of B = pi x 0.20^2 = 0.126 mm2; breaking mass per mm2 = 4.2 / 0.126 = 33 kg mm^-2.
Fibre A supports more mass per unit area before it breaks, so it has the greater tensile strength.

questions.question: Describe how stomata close when a plant is short of water, and explain one advantage and one disadvantage of this response to the plant.
questions.answer: The guard cells lose water and turgor, so the stomata close; this reduces water loss by transpiration but also reduces the carbon dioxide entering for photosynthesis.
steps: Water leaves the guard cells by osmosis, so they lose turgor and become flaccid
The stoma (pore) closes
Advantage: less water vapour is lost by transpiration, so the plant is less likely to wilt
Disadvantage: less carbon dioxide diffuses into the leaf, so the rate of photosynthesis falls
accept: Less evaporation of water from the surfaces of the mesophyll cells
Less cooling by evaporation, so the leaf temperature may rise
Guard cells have thick inner walls, so changes in turgor change the shape of the pore

questions.question: A student used a microscope to count the stomata on the lower epidermis of a leaf. The diameter of the field of view was 0.45 mm and the mean number of stomata in the field of view was 18. Calculate the stomatal density in stomata per mm2. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
questions.answer: 113 stomata per mm2
steps: Radius of the field of view = 0.45 / 2 = 0.225 mm.
Stomatal density = 18 / 0.159 = 113 stomata per mm2 (3 s.f.).

questions.question: Describe how xylem vessels and phloem sieve tube elements are each adapted for their functions.
questions.answer: Xylem vessels are dead, lignified, hollow tubes with pits; sieve tube elements have sieve plates and little cytoplasm and are supported by companion cells with many mitochondria.
steps: Xylem: walls thickened with lignin, strong and waterproof, so the vessels do not collapse and give support
Xylem vessels are dead with no cytoplasm or end walls, forming a continuous tube with little resistance to the flow of water
Pits (thin areas of wall without lignin) allow water to move sideways between vessels or into adjacent cells
Phloem: sieve plates (perforated end walls) allow the sucrose solution to flow from one sieve tube element to the next
Sieve tube elements have little cytoplasm and no nucleus, which reduces resistance to flow
Companion cells with many mitochondria (ATP for loading sucrose) are linked to the sieve tube elements by plasmodesmata
accept: Cellulose microfibrils in the xylem walls give tensile strength
Xylem vessels are hollow so water flows with little resistance
Companion cells provide metabolic support for the sieve tube elements
Plasmodesmata link the companion cells and the sieve tube elements

questions.question: A student compared the rate of water loss from three identical potted geranium plants, each with a total leaf surface area of 180 cm2. The surface of the soil in each pot was covered with plastic film. The plants were weighed at the start and after 6 hours. Plant A was kept in still air at 20 degrees C. Plant B was kept at 20 degrees C in front of a fan. Plant C was kept in still air at 30 degrees C. The mass lost was 3.6 g for plant A, 7.2 g for plant B and 5.4 g for plant C. Calculate the mean rate of water loss from plant A in g cm^-2 h^-1. Give your answer in standard form to 2 significant figures.
steps: Rate = mass lost / (leaf area x time) = 3.6 / (180 x 6) = 3.6 / 1080.

questions.question: A student compared the rate of water loss from three identical potted geranium plants, each with a total leaf surface area of 180 cm2. The surface of the soil in each pot was covered with plastic film. The plants were weighed at the start and after 6 hours. Plant A was kept in still air at 20 degrees C. Plant B was kept at 20 degrees C in front of a fan. Plant C was kept in still air at 30 degrees C. The mass lost was 3.6 g for plant A, 7.2 g for plant B and 5.4 g for plant C. Explain why plant B lost more water than plant A.
questions.answer: The fan removed water vapour from around the leaves, keeping the diffusion gradient steep, so water vapour diffused out of the stomata faster.
steps: Water vapour diffuses out of the stomata down a water potential (concentration) gradient
The fan blows away water vapour near the stomata / leaf surface, so the concentration outside stays low
The gradient is steeper, so diffusion of water vapour is faster
accept: Wind removes the layer of humid air around the leaf
The lower humidity outside the leaf increases the gradient
Faster evaporation from the mesophyll cells because of the steeper gradient

questions.question: A student compared the rate of water loss from three identical potted geranium plants, each with a total leaf surface area of 180 cm2. The surface of the soil in each pot was covered with plastic film. The plants were weighed at the start and after 6 hours. Plant A was kept in still air at 20 degrees C. Plant B was kept at 20 degrees C in front of a fan. Plant C was kept in still air at 30 degrees C. The mass lost was 3.6 g for plant A, 7.2 g for plant B and 5.4 g for plant C. Explain why plant C lost more water than plant A.
questions.answer: At the higher temperature water evaporates faster from the mesophyll cells and the air outside holds more water, so the gradient is steeper and diffusion is faster.
steps: Higher temperature gives water molecules more kinetic energy, so water evaporates faster from the mesophyll cell surfaces
Warmer air holds more water vapour (lower relative humidity), so the water potential gradient between leaf and air is steeper
Water vapour diffuses out of the stomata faster, so more water is lost
accept: Faster diffusion of water vapour molecules because of their greater kinetic energy
Replacement water is drawn up the xylem faster, so the mass lost from the plant is greater

questions.question: A student compared the rate of water loss from three identical potted geranium plants, each with a total leaf surface area of 180 cm2. The surface of the soil in each pot was covered with plastic film. The plants were weighed at the start and after 6 hours. Plant A was kept in still air at 20 degrees C. Plant B was kept at 20 degrees C in front of a fan. Plant C was kept in still air at 30 degrees C. The mass lost was 3.6 g for plant A, 7.2 g for plant B and 5.4 g for plant C. Evaluate the use of the mass lost by a whole potted plant as a measure of the rate of transpiration.
questions.answer: Covering the soil makes most of the mass lost due to transpiration, but some water is used in photosynthesis and there was no replication, so the method is only a reasonable estimate.
steps: Strength: the soil is covered, so most of the mass lost is due to transpiration
Limitation: some water is used in photosynthesis or retained in the plant, and carbon dioxide uptake and oxygen release also change the mass, so mass lost is not exactly the water transpired
Limitation: only one plant for each condition (no replicates) and the plants may differ, so the results are not reliable
accept: Simple, quantitative method using a balance
The plastic film may not be completely sealed, so some water may evaporate from the soil
Does not distinguish stomatal transpiration from water loss through the cuticle
The same leaf area and time were used, so the comparison between conditions is fair
Overall it gives a reasonable comparison between conditions but not an exact rate of transpiration

questions.question: A shoot is illuminated from one side only. Which of the following describes what happens to auxin and growth in the shoot? A Auxin accumulates on the shaded side and increases cell elongation there, so the shoot bends towards the light, B Auxin accumulates on the illuminated side and increases cell elongation there, so the shoot bends away from the light, C Auxin is destroyed on the shaded side, so the cells there elongate less and the shoot bends away from the light, D Auxin accumulates on the illuminated side and inhibits cell elongation there, so the shoot bends towards the light.
questions.answer: A: auxin accumulates on the shaded side and increases cell elongation there, so the shoot bends towards the light
steps: In a shoot illuminated from one side, auxin is moved to the shaded side.
Auxin stimulates cell elongation in the shoot, so the cells on the shaded side elongate more and the shoot bends towards the light (positive phototropism).

B, C and D all put the auxin on the wrong side or give the wrong effect: auxin does not accumulate on the illuminated side, it is not destroyed on the shaded side, and it promotes (not inhibits) elongation in shoots.

questions.question: In a germinating barley seed, gibberellin produced by the embryo has which of the following effects? A It inhibits the synthesis of amylase in the aleurone layer, B It stimulates the transcription of the gene for amylase in the aleurone layer, C It is hydrolysed by amylase to release glucose, D It converts starch in the endosperm to maltose.
questions.answer: B: it stimulates the transcription of the gene for amylase in the aleurone layer
steps: Gibberellin from the embryo diffuses to the aleurone layer and switches on (stimulates transcription of) the gene for amylase.
Amylase is then made and hydrolyses the stored starch in the endosperm to maltose.

A has the opposite effect; C is wrong because gibberellin is a plant growth substance, not a substrate of amylase; D is wrong because gibberellin is not an enzyme and amylase, not gibberellin, converts starch to maltose.

questions.question: Seedlings of a tall variety and a dwarf variety of pea were grown for 14 days. Half of each variety was sprayed with a solution of gibberellic acid each day and half was sprayed with water. The mean heights of the plants were: dwarf variety sprayed with water 12.4 cm, dwarf variety sprayed with gibberellic acid 18.9 cm, tall variety sprayed with water 38.6 cm and tall variety sprayed with gibberellic acid 39.1 cm. Calculate the percentage increase in the mean height of the dwarf variety caused by gibberellic acid. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
steps: Increase in height = 18.9 - 12.4 = 6.5 cm.
Percentage increase = 6.5 / 12.4 x 100 = 52% (2 s.f.).

questions.question: Seedlings of a tall variety and a dwarf variety of pea were grown for 14 days. Half of each variety was sprayed with a solution of gibberellic acid each day and half was sprayed with water. The mean heights of the plants were: dwarf variety sprayed with water 12.4 cm, dwarf variety sprayed with gibberellic acid 18.9 cm, tall variety sprayed with water 38.6 cm and tall variety sprayed with gibberellic acid 39.1 cm. Suggest why gibberellic acid caused a large increase in the height of the dwarf variety but almost no increase in the height of the tall variety.
questions.answer: The tall variety already makes enough gibberellin, but the dwarf variety lacks it, so added gibberellic acid lets the stem elongate.
steps: The tall variety already makes enough gibberellin for maximum stem elongation, so extra has little effect
The dwarf variety makes too little gibberellin (e.g. a mutated allele for an enzyme in its synthesis)
The added gibberellic acid stimulates cell elongation / division in the stem, so the dwarf plants grow taller
accept: The tall variety may already be at its genetically determined maximum height
Gibberellin lengthens the internodes of the stem

questions.question: Lettuce seeds were soaked in water and kept in the dark. They were then given brief flashes of red light (R) and far-red light (FR) in four different sequences. The percentage of seeds that germinated was 96% after R, 8% after R then FR, 95% after R, FR then R, and 7% after R, FR, R then FR. Explain these results.
questions.answer: Red light converts phytochrome Pr to Pfr, which stimulates germination, and far-red light converts Pfr back to Pr, so the last flash decides the result.
steps: Phytochrome exists in two forms: Pr (absorbs red light, 660 nm) and Pfr (absorbs far-red light, 730 nm)
Red light converts Pr to Pfr, and Pfr promotes germination (e.g. by switching on genes)
Far-red light converts Pfr back to Pr, so germination is not stimulated
The forms are interconverted each time, so the last flash decides the result (high germination after red, low after far-red)
accept: Pfr is the active form
Pfr slowly reverts to Pr in the dark
Lettuce seeds need light to germinate
Pfr promotes the production of gibberellin

questions.question: Explain how gibberellin allows a barley seed to use its stored starch when it germinates.
questions.answer: Water activates the embryo, which releases gibberellin; this switches on the amylase gene in the aleurone layer, and amylase hydrolyses starch to maltose and then glucose for the embryo to respire and grow.
steps: The seed absorbs water, which activates the embryo, and the embryo releases gibberellin
Gibberellin diffuses to the aleurone layer
Gibberellin stimulates the transcription of the gene for amylase
Amylase is made in the aleurone cells and secreted into the endosperm
Amylase hydrolyses starch to maltose (maltase then hydrolyses maltose to glucose)
Glucose is transported to the embryo and used in respiration to release ATP / to make cellulose for growth
accept: The seedling can grow before it is able to photosynthesise
Gibberellin acts as a signal (plant growth substance) between the embryo and the aleurone layer
Amylase is made by transcription followed by translation
Amylase breaks the glycosidic bonds in starch
Gibberellin is released in response to water uptake (imbibition)

questions.question: The tips of 20 oat coleoptiles were cut off and placed on a block of agar for two hours. Each agar block was then placed on one side of the cut top of a different coleoptile, kept in darkness. A control used blocks of agar that had not been in contact with a tip. After 90 minutes the mean angle of curvature of the coleoptiles was 14.8 degrees (away from the side with the block) when the block had been in contact with a tip and 0.6 degrees when the agar was plain. Calculate how many times greater the mean angle of curvature was with the blocks that had been in contact with tips than with plain agar blocks. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
questions.answer: 25 times
steps: = 24.7, which is 25 times to 2 s.f.

questions.question: The tips of 20 oat coleoptiles were cut off and placed on a block of agar for two hours. Each agar block was then placed on one side of the cut top of a different coleoptile, kept in darkness. A control used blocks of agar that had not been in contact with a tip. After 90 minutes the mean angle of curvature of the coleoptiles was 14.8 degrees (away from the side with the block) when the block had been in contact with a tip and 0.6 degrees when the agar was plain. Explain why the coleoptiles bent away from the side with the agar block.
questions.answer: Auxin from the tip diffused into the agar and then into one side of the coleoptile only, so the cells on that side elongated more and the coleoptile bent away from the block.
steps: The tip produces auxin, which diffuses into the agar block
Auxin diffuses from the block into one side of the coleoptile only
Auxin stimulates cell elongation on that side, so that side grows more and the coleoptile bends away from the block
accept: Cells on the side without auxin elongate less
Unequal growth causes the curvature
Auxin moves down to the elongating cells below the tip

questions.question: The tips of 20 oat coleoptiles were cut off and placed on a block of agar for two hours. Each agar block was then placed on one side of the cut top of a different coleoptile, kept in darkness. A control used blocks of agar that had not been in contact with a tip. After 90 minutes the mean angle of curvature of the coleoptiles was 14.8 degrees (away from the side with the block) when the block had been in contact with a tip and 0.6 degrees when the agar was plain. Explain why the investigation was carried out in darkness and why plain agar blocks were used as a control.
questions.answer: Darkness stops light affecting where auxin moves; plain agar shows that curvature is caused by a substance from the tip and not by the agar or the block.
steps: Darkness: light would redistribute the auxin (phototropism), so only the position of the block affects curvature
Plain agar control shows that the curvature is due to a substance from the tip, not the agar or the placing of a block
accept: The control keeps all other variables the same (size of block, time, position)
Darkness removes light as a variable, which improves validity
Shows that the agar does not cause bending by itself

questions.question: The tips of 20 oat coleoptiles were cut off and placed on a block of agar for two hours. Each agar block was then placed on one side of the cut top of a different coleoptile, kept in darkness. A control used blocks of agar that had not been in contact with a tip. After 90 minutes the mean angle of curvature of the coleoptiles was 14.8 degrees (away from the side with the block) when the block had been in contact with a tip and 0.6 degrees when the agar was plain. In a second experiment, a coleoptile tip was placed on two separate agar blocks divided by a thin sheet of mica, and light shone from one side. The block under the shaded side collected 65% of the auxin and the block under the lit side collected 35%. In a control in darkness, each block collected 50% of the auxin, and the total amount collected was the same in both experiments. Explain what these results show about the effect of one-sided light on auxin.
questions.answer: One-sided light does not destroy auxin but causes it to move across the tip from the lit side to the shaded side.
steps: The total auxin was the same in light and in darkness, so light does not destroy auxin or stop it being made
More auxin (65%) was collected from the shaded side, so one-sided light makes auxin move across the tip to the shaded side
Greater auxin concentration on the shaded side causes greater elongation there, explaining bending towards the light (phototropism)
accept: 50 : 50 in darkness shows an even distribution of auxin without light
Lateral transport of auxin across the tip from the lit side to the shaded side
Light does not inhibit auxin production in the tip
The unequal distribution of auxin in the tip causes unequal growth on the two sides
